questions.stem:
Consider the following statements :
1. In the first Lok Sabha, the single largest party in the opposition was the Swatantra Party.
2. In the Lok Sabha, a "Leader of the Opposition" was recognised for the first time in 1969.
3. In the Lok Sabha, if a party does not have a minimum of 75 members, its leader cannot be recognised as the Leader of the Opposition.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct ?
questions.explanation_md:
**1 — wrong.** The **Swatantra Party was founded only in 1959 (by C. Rajagopalachari), so it could not exist in the First Lok Sabha (1952–57)**; the largest opposition party then was the **CPI (16 seats)**.

**2 — correct.** The post was first *recognised* in the Lok Sabha in **1969**, when **Ram Subhag Singh (Congress-O)** was given the title. Statutory status came later, via the **Salary and Allowances of Leaders of Opposition in Parliament Act, 1977**.

**3 — wrong.** The threshold is **not 75**. By the Speaker's direction (Mavalankar convention, 1956) the party must have at least **1/10th of the total strength of the House = 55 members** in the Lok Sabha. This is why there was **no recognised LoP in the 16th and 17th Lok Sabhas**.

Only 2 is correct.

questions.stem:
Which of the following leaf modifications occur(s) in the desert areas to inhibit water loss ?
1. Hard and waxy leaves
2. Tiny leaves
3. Thorns instead of leaves
Select the correct answer using the code given below :
questions.explanation_md:
All three are genuine **xerophytic adaptations that cut transpiration**.

1. **Hard, thick, waxy leaves** — a heavy **cuticle** is water-impermeable and reflects heat (e.g. *Nerium*, *Acacia*). Correct.
2. **Tiny leaves** — reducing leaf area reduces the surface from which water evaporates (e.g. *Casuarina*, *Tamarix*). Correct.
3. **Thorns/spines instead of leaves** — in **Opuntia and other cacti the leaves are reduced to spines and the stem (phylloclade) takes over photosynthesis**; spines have almost no stomata and also trap a still boundary layer of air. Correct.

Since all three reduce water loss, the answer is **1, 2 and 3**.
questions.tagging_note: Xerophytic leaf adaptations. No topic in the tree covers plant physiology/botany directly — SNT-01 'Basic biology' is scoped to cell, genetics, human systems and nutrition, so it does not really cover plant adaptation. ENV-03 (desert terrestrial ecosystems) and GEO-11 (natural vegetation) are the closest genuine fits; this is a small gap in the syllabus tree for pure NCERT botany.

questions.stem:
As per the NSSO 70th Round "Situation Assessment Survey of Agricultural Households", consider the following statements :
1. Rajasthan has the highest percentage share of agricultural households among its rural households.
2. Out of the total agricultural households in the country, a little over 60 percent belong to OBCs.
3. In Kerala, a little over 60 percent of agricultural households reported to have received maximum income from sources other than agricultural activities.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct ?
questions.explanation_md:
NSSO **70th Round (2013), Situation Assessment Survey of Agricultural Households**.

**1 — correct.** **Rajasthan had the highest share of agricultural households among rural households (~78%)**, ahead of UP and MP.

**2 — wrong.** The **OBC share of agricultural households was about 45%**, not "a little over 60%". Roughly: OBC ~45%, Others ~26%, SC ~16%, ST ~13%. The 60% figure is the trap.

**3 — correct.** **Kerala is the classic outlier — around 61% of its agricultural households drew their maximum income from non-agricultural sources** (wages, remittances, non-farm business), reflecting its small holdings and remittance economy.

So 1 and 3 only.
questions.tagging_note: NSSO Situation Assessment Survey of Agricultural Households — agricultural household income and composition data. Sits between agri-economy (ECO-14) and Indian agriculture geography (GEO-17); no topic covers NSSO survey rounds/statistical system as such.

questions.stem:
How is the National Green Tribunal (NGT) different from the Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) ?
1. The NGT has been established by an Act whereas the CPCB has been created by an executive order of the Government.
2. The NGT provides environmental justice and helps reduce the burden of litigation in the higher courts whereas the CPCB promotes cleanliness of streams and wells, and aims to improve the quality of air in the country.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct ?
questions.explanation_md:
**1 — wrong.** Both are **statutory**, not one statutory and one executive. NGT: **National Green Tribunal Act, 2010** (Art. 21, 48A, 51A(g) and the Stockholm/Rio commitments). CPCB: **constituted under the Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974**, and later given functions under the Air Act, 1981. So the CPCB was **not** created by an executive order.

**2 — correct.** The NGT is a **specialised judicial body for effective and expeditious disposal of environment cases (6 months limit), reducing the load on High Courts and the Supreme Court**. The CPCB's statutory mandate is exactly "to **promote cleanliness of streams and wells** and to **improve the quality of air**".

Only 2 is correct.

questions.stem:
Consider the following statements :
1. The Parliament of India can place a particular law in the Ninth Schedule of the Constitution of India.
2. The validity of a law placed in the Ninth Schedule cannot be examined by any court and no judgement can be made on it.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct ?
questions.explanation_md:
**1 — correct.** Parliament can add a law to the **Ninth Schedule**, but only through a **constitutional amendment under Article 368** (the Schedule itself was inserted by the **1st Amendment, 1951**, along with Article 31B).

**2 — wrong.** Article 31B gives blanket immunity on paper, but **I.R. Coelho v. State of Tamil Nadu (2007)** held that **any law placed in the Ninth Schedule after 24 April 1973 (the date of the Kesavananda Bharati judgement) is open to judicial review if it violates the basic structure or abridges Articles 14, 19, 20, 21**. So courts *can* examine such laws.

Only 1 is correct.
questions.tagging_note: Ninth Schedule + judicial reviewability turns on I.R. Coelho, hence POL-13 primary; the insertion mechanism is Art 368 (POL-12) and the Schedules themselves sit in POL-03.

questions.stem: Which one of the following best describes the term "Merchant Discount Rate" sometimes seen in news ?
options: The incentive given by a bank to a merchant for accepting payments through debit cards pertaining to that bank.
The amount paid back by banks to their customers when they use debit cards for financial transactions for purchasing goods or services.
The charge to a merchant by a bank for accepting payments from his customers through the bank's debit cards.
The incentive given by the Government to merchants for promoting digital payments by their customers through Point of Sale (PoS) machines and debit cards.
questions.explanation_md:
**MDR = the fee a merchant pays (deducted from the sale value) to the acquiring bank for processing a card/digital payment.** It is expressed as a percentage of the transaction and is **shared between the acquiring bank, the issuing bank (interchange) and the card network/payment system**.

Key point: it is a **cost to the merchant, never to the customer** — RBI rules bar merchants from passing it on as a surcharge. RBI caps MDR for debit cards by merchant turnover, and MDR on **RuPay debit cards and BHIM-UPI was made zero from 1 January 2020**.

(a) and (d) invert it into an incentive; (b) describes cashback. Answer (c).
questions.tagging_note: Merchant Discount Rate is a digital-payments term; ECO-20 (UPI/new economy payments) is the closest fit, with ECO-04 for the banking-side charge. No dedicated payment-systems topic exists in the tree.

questions.stem:
What is/are the consequence/consequences of a country becoming the member of the 'Nuclear Suppliers Group' ?
1. It will have access to the latest and most efficient nuclear technologies.
2. It automatically becomes a member of "The Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons (NPT)".
Which of the statements given above is/are correct ?
questions.explanation_md:
**1 — correct.** The **NSG is a 48-member export-control cartel; membership gives access to controlled nuclear technology, fuel and dual-use equipment through the guidelines-based trade regime** and a seat in framing those guidelines. That is precisely why India seeks entry.

**2 — wrong.** **The NSG and the NPT are entirely separate instruments — joining the NSG does not make a country an NPT signatory.** The NSG was itself created *after* the 1974 Indian test because the NPT alone had proved inadequate; NPT accession is a sovereign act of signing and ratifying that treaty. (India is not an NPT member and got a **clean NSG waiver in 2008** without joining it.)

Only 1 is correct.
questions.tagging_note: NSG is an export-control regime and NPT a treaty, so CAI-07 (treaties/global governance) fits best; CAI-04 covers it as a multilateral grouping. Straddles S&T (SNT-08 nuclear) only lightly.

questions.stem:
With reference to India's decision to levy an equalization tax of 6% on online advertisement services offered by non-resident entities, which of the following statements is/are correct ?
1. It is introduced as a part of the Income Tax Act.
2. Non-resident entities that offer advertisement services in India can claim a tax credit in their home country under the "Double Taxation Avoidance Agreements".
Select the correct answer using the code given below :
questions.explanation_md:
**1 — wrong.** The **6% equalisation levy was introduced by Chapter VIII of the Finance Act, 2016 as a standalone levy — deliberately kept OUTSIDE the Income Tax Act, 1961.** It applies to B2B payments above Rs 1 lakh a year to non-residents for online advertisement and related digital ad space (the "Google tax").

**2 — wrong, and it follows from 1.** Because the levy is **not an income tax under the IT Act, it falls outside the scope of DTAAs**, which cover taxes on income. So the non-resident **cannot claim foreign tax credit** for it at home — the main criticism of the design, since it creates double taxation.

Neither statement is correct.
questions.tagging_note: Equalisation levy is a taxation question (ECO-11); the DTAA/credit limb touches the external sector (ECO-12).

questions.stem:
Consider the following statements :
1. The Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management (FRBM) Review Committee Report has recommended a debt to GDP ratio of 60% for the general (combined) government by 2023, comprising 40% for the Central Government and 20% for the State Governments.
2. The Central Government has domestic liabilities of 21% of GDP as compared to that of 49% of GDP of the State Governments.
3. As per the Constitution of India, it is mandatory for a State to take the Central Government's consent for raising any loan if the former owes any outstanding liabilities to the latter.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct ?
questions.explanation_md:
**FRBM Review Committee = N. K. Singh Committee (report submitted January 2017).**

**1 — correct.** It recommended a **general government debt-to-GDP ceiling of 60% by 2023 — 40% Centre + 20% States** — treating debt as the primary anchor and the fiscal deficit (3% by 2020) as the operational target.

**2 — wrong; the figures are reversed.** **The Centre's domestic liabilities were about 49% of GDP and the States' about 21%** — which is exactly why the 40:20 split was proposed.

**3 — correct.** **Article 293(3): a State cannot raise any loan without the Centre's consent if any part of a loan made to it by the Centre is still outstanding**, and under 293(4) the Centre may attach conditions to that consent.

So 1 and 3 only.
questions.tagging_note: Statements 1-2 are FRBM/fiscal (ECO-10); statement 3 is Art 293 State borrowing, a Centre-State financial relations point (POL-15) — genuine cross-subject straddle.

questions.stem:
Consider the following statements :
1. The quantity of imported edible oils is more than the domestic production of edible oils in the last five years.
2. The Government does not impose any customs duty on all the imported edible oils as a special case.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct ?
questions.explanation_md:
**1 — correct.** **India imports roughly 60–70% of its edible oil requirement — about 15 million tonnes imported against domestic production of only 7–8 million tonnes.** So imports have exceeded domestic output every year (palm oil from Indonesia/Malaysia, soya from Argentina/Brazil, sunflower from Ukraine/Russia). Edible oil is one of India's largest import bills after crude and gold.

**2 — wrong.** **Customs duty is very much levied on imported edible oils, and is actively used as a policy lever** — import duties were raised sharply in 2017–18 (crude palm oil to 44%, refined to 54%) precisely to protect domestic oilseed growers. There is no blanket exemption.

Only 1 is correct.
questions.tagging_note: Edible oil import dependence (ECO-14 agriculture) plus the customs-duty limb, which is trade/tariff policy — ECO-12 external sector is the nearest fit since ECO-11 taxation is framed around direct/indirect/GST rather than customs tariffs.

questions.stem: He wrote biographies of Mazzini, Garibaldi, Shivaji and Shrikrishna; stayed in America for some time; and was also elected to the Central Assembly. He was
questions.explanation_md:
**Lala Lajpat Rai** wrote biographies of Mazzini, Garibaldi, Shivaji and Shri Krishna (also *Unhappy India*). He was in the **USA 1914–1920**, where he founded the Indian Home Rule League of America and edited *Young India*; he was **elected to the Central Legislative Assembly in 1926**, and died in 1928 of lathi injuries at the Simon Commission protest in Lahore.

Quick eliminations: Aurobindo left politics for Pondicherry (1910) and never sat in the Assembly; Bipin Chandra Pal went to **England**, not America; Motilal Nehru was in the Assembly (Swaraj Party leader) but wrote no such biographies.

questions.stem:
Consider the following statements :
1. Aadhaar card can be used as a proof of citizenship or domicile.
2. Once issued, Aadhaar number cannot be deactivated or omitted by the Issuing Authority.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct ?
questions.explanation_md:
Both statements are wrong.

1. **Wrong.** Aadhaar is proof of **identity, not of citizenship or domicile** — UIDAI states this explicitly, and residents (including foreigners resident 182+ days) are eligible. The Aadhaar Act enrols *residents*, not citizens.
2. **Wrong.** **Section 23(2)(g) of the Aadhaar Act, 2016** empowers UIDAI to specify conditions for **omitting and deactivating** an Aadhaar number — e.g. biometric-quality failures, duplicate enrolment, death, or a child not updating biometrics at 5/15.

Answer: **Neither 1 nor 2**.
questions.tagging_note: No dedicated Aadhaar/UIDAI topic in the vocabulary. POL-27 (e-governance) is the nearest home; POL-06 is included only because statement 1 tests that Aadhaar is not proof of citizenship.

questions.stem:
Which of the following has/have shrunk immensely/dried up in the recent past due to human activities ?
1. Aral Sea
2. Black Sea
3. Lake Baikal
Select the correct answer using the code given below :
questions.explanation_md:
1. **Aral Sea — correct.** The classic textbook case of human-caused desiccation: Soviet diversion of the **Amu Darya and Syr Darya** for cotton irrigation from the 1960s shrank it to a fraction of its area; the eastern South Aral basin went dry in 2014.
2. **Black Sea — wrong.** A large marine basin connected to the Mediterranean via the Bosphorus; polluted and eutrophic, but not shrinking.
3. **Lake Baikal — wrong.** The world's **deepest and largest-by-volume** freshwater lake (~20% of unfrozen surface freshwater); it faces pollution and shoreline stress, not drying up.

Answer: **1 only**.
questions.tagging_note: Gap: the tree has no topic for world lakes / inland water bodies. GEO-10 is oceans only, GEO-11 is biomes. GEO-24 (atlas drills, places in news) is the only genuine fit for a world-lakes location question.

questions.stem: "Rule of Law Index" is released by which of the following ?
options: The Office of UN Commissioner for Human Rights
questions.explanation_md:
The **Rule of Law Index** is published by the **World Justice Project (WJP)**, an independent US-based NGO, annually since 2010. It scores countries on eight factors — constraints on government powers, absence of corruption, open government, fundamental rights, order and security, regulatory enforcement, civil justice, criminal justice.

Note the related trap: Amnesty International puts out an annual human-rights report; the OHCHR does not publish this index; the ICJ (The Hague) settles inter-state disputes and publishes no index.

questions.stem: Which one of the following links all the ATMs in India ?
questions.explanation_md:
**NPCI** operates the **National Financial Switch (NFS)**, the network that interconnects India's ATMs and enables interbank cash withdrawal. NFS was built by **IDRBT** and transferred to NPCI in **2009**.

NPCI is an umbrella retail-payments body set up in 2008 by RBI and IBA under Section 25 of the Companies Act; it also runs **RuPay, UPI, IMPS, NACH, AePS, BBPS, FASTag (NETC)**. RBI is the regulator, not the operator; IBA is a bankers' association; NSDL is a securities depository.
questions.tagging_note: NPCI is retail-payments infrastructure (National Financial Switch), so ECO-20 (UPI/new economy payments) fits better than ECO-04, which is about bank categories rather than payment system operators.

questions.stem:
Consider the following statements :
1. Capital Adequacy Ratio (CAR) is the amount that banks have to maintain in the form of their own funds to offset any loss that banks incur if the account-holders fail to repay dues.
2. CAR is decided by each individual bank.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct ?
questions.explanation_md:
1. **Correct.** CAR (capital-to-risk-weighted-assets ratio) is the bank's **own capital** — Tier 1 + Tier 2 as a proportion of risk-weighted assets — held as a cushion so that **depositors are protected when borrowers default**.
2. **Wrong.** CAR is prescribed by the **RBI**, not by each bank. Under Basel III, RBI mandates a minimum of **9%** for Indian scheduled commercial banks (above Basel's 8%), plus a capital conservation buffer.

Answer: **1 only**.
questions.tagging_note: CAR is a Basel norm (ECO-05); ECO-03 included because the RBI prescribes it, which is what statement 2 tests.

questions.stem:
The identity platform 'Aadhaar' provides open "Application Programming Interfaces (APIs)". What does it imply ?
1. It can be integrated into any electronic device.
2. Online authentication using iris is possible.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct ?
questions.explanation_md:
**"Open API" is a statement about the interface, not about how many devices happen to use it. Both implications follow, so (c).**

Aadhaar authentication is published by UIDAI as an **open, stateless, HTTPS request-response API**: the specification is public, the payload is plain XML/JSON, and it carries **no dependency on any operating system, hardware vendor or form factor**. That device- and platform-neutrality is the whole meaning of "open" here.

**Statement 1 - correct.** Because the spec is public and platform-agnostic, the authentication call can be built into **any electronic device** that can reach the CIDR: a mobile phone, a tablet, a PoS terminal, a micro-ATM, a handheld enrolment kit, a bank kiosk, an attendance terminal. Note precisely what the statement claims - that the **API can be integrated into** a device, not that every device already performs Aadhaar authentication or can do so without a sensor or connectivity. The tempting reading is to treat "any" as an absolute empirical claim and reject it; but "integrable into any device" is exactly the property an open API confers, and it is how UIDAI itself describes the authentication API.

**Statement 2 - correct.** Aadhaar authentication accepts **demographic, OTP and biometric** factors, and biometric under the Aadhaar Act 2016 is defined as **photograph, fingerprint and iris**. UIDAI enabled **online iris-based authentication** through Authentication API 2.0 with STQC-certified iris devices, so iris authentication over the network is available, not merely fingerprint.

**Why (b) fails:** it accepts iris but denies statement 1, which is the more direct consequence of openness. An API being open is precisely what makes it freely embeddable across devices and applications by any requesting entity; denying statement 1 would leave "open" meaning nothing at all. With both statements true, the answer is **(c) Both 1 and 2**.
questions.tagging_note: Straddles governance and IT. The stem is a digital-identity/e-governance platform question (POL-27) but the testable content is API and biometric-authentication technology (SNT-09).
questions.review_flag: Official key says c, worked solution said b (medium confidence).

questions.stem: Very recently, in which of the following countries have lakhs of people either suffered from severe famine/acute malnutrition or died due to starvation caused by war/ethnic conflicts ?
questions.explanation_md:
**Yemen and South Sudan.** In **February 2017 the UN formally declared famine in parts of Unity State, South Sudan** — the first famine declaration anywhere since Somalia 2011 — driven by civil war since 2013. **Yemen**, in civil war since 2015 with a blockade on Hodeidah port, was called by the UN the **world's worst humanitarian crisis**, with millions facing famine conditions plus a record cholera outbreak.

The other pairs had no war-driven mass starvation in that period; Venezuela's crisis was economic, not famine declared by the UN.
questions.tagging_note: Gap: no topic covers world conflicts/humanitarian crises as such. The CAI tree is India-relations-centric, so CAI-03 (West Asia/Africa) is a stretch; GEO-24 places-in-news carries the map recall (Yemen, South Sudan). Consider a 'world conflicts and crises' topic if more such PYQs appear.

questions.stem:
Regarding Wood's Dispatch, which of the following statements are true ?
1. Grants-in-Aid system was introduced.
2. Establishment of universities was recommended.
3. English as a medium of instruction at all levels of education was recommended.
Select the correct answer using the code given below :
questions.explanation_md:
**Wood's Despatch, 1854** — the "Magna Carta of English education in India", from Charles Wood, President of the Board of Control.

1. **True.** It introduced the **grants-in-aid system** to support private/aided schools, subject to inspection and secular instruction.
2. **True.** It recommended **universities on the London model**, leading to **Calcutta, Bombay and Madras universities in 1857**.
3. **False.** It prescribed a **graded system**: **vernacular languages at primary/school level**, **English at higher levels** — not English at *all* levels. This is the deciding statement.

It also asked for departments of public instruction in five provinces, teacher-training institutions, women's and vocational education.

Answer: **1 and 2 only**.
questions.tagging_note: Wood's Dispatch 1854 sits in the education strand (HIS-16); HIS-03 covers the 1773-1858 administrative period it falls in.

questions.stem: With reference to the Parliament of India, which of the following Parliamentary Committees scrutinizes and reports to the House whether the powers to make regulations, rules, sub-rules, by-laws, etc. conferred by the Constitution or delegated by the Parliament are being properly exercised by the Executive within the scope of such delegation ?
questions.explanation_md:
The **Committee on Subordinate Legislation** examines whether the **executive is properly exercising delegated legislative power** — rules, regulations, sub-rules, by-laws framed under the Constitution or under an Act of Parliament. Lok Sabha's has **15 members**, so does the Rajya Sabha's; it guards against excessive delegation.

Distinguish the others: **Committee on Government Assurances** tracks promises ministers make on the floor; **Rules Committee** deals with the House's own procedure rules; **Business Advisory Committee** allocates time for legislative business.

questions.stem:
Consider the following statements :
1. As per the Right to Education (RTE) Act, to be eligible for appointment as a teacher in a State, a person would be required to possess the minimum qualification laid down by the concerned State Council of Teacher Education.
2. As per the RTE Act, for teaching primary classes, a candidate is required to pass a Teacher Eligibility Test conducted in accordance with the National Council of Teacher Education guidelines.
3. In India, more than 90% of teacher education institutions are directly under the State Governments.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct ?
questions.explanation_md:
**Statement 1 — wrong.** Under **Section 23(1) of the RTE Act, 2009, the minimum qualifications for teachers are laid down by the academic authority notified by the *Central* Government — the NCTE**, not the State Council of Teacher Education. States cannot set their own minimum qualification (a State can only relax it, and only with Central permission under Sec 23(2)).

**Statement 2 — correct.** NCTE's notification under Sec 23(1) makes passing the **Teacher Eligibility Test (TET), conducted per NCTE guidelines**, a mandatory qualification for teaching Classes I–VIII (CTET/State TET).

**Statement 3 — wrong.** Teacher education in India is overwhelmingly **private/self-financed — roughly 90%+ of TEIs are private unaided**, not under State Governments. (This lopsided privatisation is exactly what the Justice Verma Committee, 2012 flagged.)

Only 2 is right.
questions.tagging_note: GAP: no topic in the tree covers education policy or the RTE Act (teacher qualifications, NCTE/State Councils of Teacher Education, teacher-education institutions). ECO-18 is the only shelf that mentions education at all, and it is an indicators topic (HDI/MPI), not a law-and-institutions one; POL-27 governance is a distant second. A dedicated 'education and social sector legislation' topic would be the honest home for this.

questions.stem:
Consider the following pairs :

| | *Tradition* | *State* |
|---|---|---|
| 1. | Chapchar Kut festival | Mizoram |
| 2. | Khongjom Parba ballad | Manipur |
| 3. | Thang-Ta dance | Sikkim |

Which of the pairs given above is/are correct ?
questions.explanation_md:
**1. Chapchar Kut – Mizoram — correct.** The biggest Mizo festival, held in March after the bamboo forest is cut and left to dry for jhum; famous for the *Cheraw* (bamboo) dance.

**2. Khongjom Parba – Manipur — correct.** A **ballad form narrating the 1891 Anglo-Manipuri War battle of Khongjom**, sung by a single performer with the *dholak*.

**3. Thang-Ta – Sikkim — wrong.** Thang-Ta (*thang* = sword, *ta* = spear) is the **Manipuri martial art**, not Sikkimese.

Easy shortcut: all three are Manipur/Mizoram items, so any pair naming Sikkim fails → 1 and 2.
questions.tagging_note: Chapchar Kut is a festival and Thang-Ta a martial art (both ART-09); Khongjom Parba is a ballad/folk performance and Thang-Ta is also performed as a dance form, hence ART-07. Matches the 2017 Q70 traditions/communities precedent (ART-09 primary).
questions.transcription_note: In the original the pairs are laid out as a two-column list with italic headings 'Tradition' and 'State', each pair joined by an em dash; rendered here as a markdown table. Verified against p-11: all three pairs and both column headings present and correctly aligned.

questions.stem:
Consider the following statements :
1. The Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 replaced the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954.
2. The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) is under the charge of Director General of Health Services in the Union Ministry of Health and Family Welfare.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct ?
questions.explanation_md:
**Statement 1 — correct.** The **Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 consolidated and repealed eight older laws, including the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954** (also the Fruit Products Order, Meat Food Products Order, Milk & Milk Products Order, Vegetable Oil Products Order, etc.).

**Statement 2 — wrong.** FSSAI is a **statutory autonomous body headed by a Chairperson (of Secretary rank) and a CEO**, administered by the Ministry of Health & Family Welfare — it is **not under the Director General of Health Services**.

Only 1.
questions.tagging_note: Follows the 2016 Q34 food-safety precedent (SNT-04, 'health missions, drug regulation and public health'). The second statement is really about the administrative structure of a statutory regulator, which no topic covers — POL-25 lists only NITI Aayog, NHRC, CIC, CVC, CBI and Lokpal, so FSSAI has no shelf there.

questions.stem: The term "two-state solution" is sometimes mentioned in the news in the context of the affairs of
questions.explanation_md:
**"Two-state solution" = Israel–Palestine.** It refers to creating an **independent State of Palestine (West Bank + Gaza, capital East Jerusalem) alongside Israel**, along roughly the pre-1967 lines — the framework behind the Oslo Accords (1993) and UNGA Resolution 181's original partition logic.

So the context is **Israel**. (Iraq/Yemen news is about civil conflict and federalism/Houthi control, not a two-state formula; China's is a "One China" issue.)
questions.tagging_note: West Asia / Israel-Palestine, same placement as the 2023 Q94 Israel question (CAI-03 primary, CAI-07 second).

questions.stem:
With reference to the provisions made under the National Food Security Act, 2013, consider the following statements :
1. The families coming under the category of 'below poverty line (BPL)' only are eligible to receive subsidised food grains.
2. The eldest woman in a household, of age 18 years or above, shall be the head of the household for the purpose of issuance of a ration card.
3. Pregnant women and lactating mothers are entitled to a 'take-home ration' of 1600 calories per day during pregnancy and for six months thereafter.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct ?
questions.explanation_md:
**Statement 1 — wrong.** NFSA 2013 abandoned the BPL/APL basis. It covers **up to 75% of rural and 50% of urban population (~two-thirds of India)** under two categories: **priority households (5 kg/person/month) and Antyodaya Anna Yojana (35 kg/household)** — not BPL only.

**Statement 2 — correct.** **Section 13: the eldest woman of the household, aged 18 or above, shall be the head of household for issuing the ration card.**

**Statement 3 — wrong.** Pregnant and lactating mothers get free meals plus a maternity benefit of ₹6,000; the **take-home ration norm is 600 calories** (not 1600) — the 1600-calorie figure is for severely malnourished children under ICDS norms.

Only 2.

questions.stem: India enacted The Geographical Indications of Goods (Registration and Protection) Act, 1999 in order to comply with the obligations to
questions.explanation_md:
India passed the GI Act, 1999 to meet its obligations under the **WTO's TRIPS Agreement (Articles 22–24 deal with geographical indications)**, which every WTO member had to implement in domestic law.

The Act came into force in 2003; **Darjeeling tea was India's first registered GI**. The same TRIPS compliance drive produced the Patents (Amendment) Acts, the Trade Marks Act 1999 and the Designs Act 2000.
questions.tagging_note: The fact actually tested is the WTO/TRIPS obligation (ECO-13, international institutions), with the GI/IPR subject matter sitting in ECO-15. Consistent with 2017 Q83 (WTO TFA -> ECO-13) and 2017 Q34 (IPR policy -> ECO-15 + ECO-13).

questions.stem:
Consider the following statements :
1. In India, State Governments do not have the power to auction non-coal mines.
2. Andhra Pradesh and Jharkhand do not have gold mines.
3. Rajasthan has iron ore mines.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct ?
questions.explanation_md:
**Statement 1 — wrong.** Under the **MMDR Amendment Act, 2015, State Governments grant mineral concessions by auction (e-auction) for non-coal minerals** — coal is the Centre's domain. States very much do auction non-coal mines.

**Statement 2 — wrong.** Both states have gold: **Andhra Pradesh has gold deposits/mining at Ramagiri (Anantapur)** and **Jharkhand has gold in the Subarnarekha belt (Sonapet/Singhbhum)**. Karnataka (Hutti, KGF) is the main producer, but the statement is an absolute denial and fails.

**Statement 3 — correct.** **Rajasthan has iron ore deposits — Morija-Banola (Jaipur), Dalli (Nagaur), Neemla, Bhilwara/Jhunjhunu belts.** Low grade compared with Odisha–Jharkhand, but they exist and are mined.

Only 3.
questions.tagging_note: Mineral distribution (gold, iron ore) is GEO-18; statement 1 on State Governments' power to auction non-coal mines is centre-state resource jurisdiction under the MMDR Act (POL-15). Same pairing as 2025 Q89, which asks almost the identical thing.

questions.stem:
With reference to digital payments, consider the following statements :
1. BHIM app allows the user to transfer money to anyone with a UPI-enabled bank account.
2. While a chip-pin debit card has four factors of authentication, BHIM app has only two factors of authentication.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct ?
questions.explanation_md:
**Statement 1 — correct.** **BHIM runs on UPI, so it can send money to any UPI-enabled bank account** — via UPI ID/VPA, mobile number, or account number + IFSC.

**Statement 2 — wrong.** A **chip-and-PIN debit card has two factors** (the card = something you have, the PIN = something you know), not four. **BHIM also has two factors** (device/SIM binding + UPI PIN). So the contrast drawn in the statement is false — both are two-factor.

Only 1.
questions.tagging_note: UPI/BHIM sits in ECO-20 (new economy), matching 2017 Q43 and 2026 Q90. The authentication-factors half of statement 2 is payment security, which is closer to SNT-10, but the question is answered from digital-payments knowledge, so ECO-06 (financial inclusion) is the more useful second tag.

questions.stem: Among the following cities, which one lies on a longitude closest to that of Delhi ?
questions.explanation_md:
**Answer: (a) Bengaluru**

The question asks about **longitude** — the east–west coordinate, the meridian a city sits on. It says nothing about distance from Delhi. Read it as "which city is most nearly due north–south of Delhi", not "which city is nearest Delhi".

Approximate coordinates:

| City | Longitude | Gap from Delhi (77°13′E) |
|---|---|---|
| Delhi | 77°13′E (77.2°) | — |
| **Bengaluru** | **77°35′E (77.6°)** | **≈ 0.4°** |
| Hyderabad | 78°29′E (78.5°) | ≈ 1.3° |
| Nagpur | 79°05′E (79.1°) | ≈ 1.9° |
| Pune | 73°51′E (73.9°) | ≈ 3.3° |

Bengaluru is roughly 1,750 km from Delhi — by far the farthest of the four — yet it lies almost exactly on Delhi's meridian, under half a degree east. The Delhi–Bengaluru line is very nearly a straight north–south line down the country (the Srinagar–Kanyakumari NH-44 corridor runs close to it). Distance and longitude are independent here, and the question only asks for longitude.

**Why (c) Nagpur fails.** Nagpur is the tempting choice because it is the standard "centre of India" city — the Zero Mile Stone, the Tropic of Cancer passing just to its north, the point every map calls central. But *central* is a statement about being near the middle in **both** coordinates; it is not a statement about sharing Delhi's meridian. Nagpur sits at 79°05′E, nearly 2° — about 190 km of east–west offset — east of Delhi. Hyderabad, at 78°29′E, is actually closer to Delhi's meridian than Nagpur is, so even the runner-up reasoning does not land on (c). Pune, at 73°51′E, is the farthest off, over 3° west.

The trap is substituting "most central / closest to Delhi in a general sense" for the precise term **longitude**. Once the question is read as strictly a meridian comparison, Bengaluru wins on the numbers with no ambiguity.

*Memory hook: Delhi 77°E, Bengaluru 77°E — far apart, same meridian.*
questions.tagging_note: Pure atlas recall of Indian city positions (GEO-24), resting on the longitude concept from GEO-01.
questions.review_flag: Official key says a, worked solution said c (high confidence).

questions.stem: International Labour Organization's Conventions 138 and 182 are related to
options: Adaptation of agricultural practices to global climate change
Regulation of food prices and food security
questions.explanation_md:
**ILO Convention 138 (1973) — Minimum Age for Admission to Employment** (general minimum 15, light work 13, hazardous 18).

**ILO Convention 182 (1999) — Worst Forms of Child Labour** (slavery, trafficking, forced recruitment, prostitution, illicit activities, hazardous work).

Both are **child labour** conventions, and **India ratified both in June 2017**, which is why they were in the news before this paper. C-138 and C-182 are two of the ILO's eight core/fundamental conventions.
questions.tagging_note: GAP: the ILO has no topic of its own — ECO-13 names only IMF, World Bank, WTO, ADB and NDB, and labour law / labour standards were already flagged as a gap at 2021 Q2. CAI-07 (treaties and conventions) is the nearest genuine shelf for 'which body issued these conventions'; ECO-17 carries the child-labour/employment subject matter.

questions.stem: Regarding Money Bill, which of the following statements is **not** correct ?
options: A bill shall be deemed to be a Money Bill if it contains only provisions relating to imposition, abolition, remission, alteration or regulation of any tax.
A Money Bill has provisions for the custody of the Consolidated Fund of India or the Contingency Fund of India.
A Money Bill is concerned with the appropriation of moneys out of the Contingency Fund of India.
A Money Bill deals with the regulation of borrowing of money or giving of any guarantee by the Government of India.
questions.explanation_md:
**Article 110(1)** defines a Money Bill. Test each option against its clauses:

- **(a) Correct as stated.** Art. 110(1)(a): imposition, abolition, remission, alteration or regulation of any tax. The word "only" in the stem mirrors the Article's own opening — a Bill is a Money Bill if it contains *only* provisions dealing with all or any of the listed matters.
- **(b) Correct.** Art. 110(1)(d): "the custody of the Consolidated Fund or the **Contingency Fund of India**, the payment of moneys into or the withdrawal of moneys from any such Fund." Custody covers *both* funds.
- **(c) NOT correct.** Art. 110(1)(c) speaks of appropriation of moneys **out of the Consolidated Fund of India**, not the Contingency Fund. **Appropriation is only ever from the Consolidated Fund** — the Contingency Fund is an imprest at the disposal of the President for unforeseen expenditure, and money spent from it is later recouped by an appropriation from the Consolidated Fund. Custody of the Contingency Fund is a Money Bill matter; appropriation *out of* it is not.
- **(d) Correct.** Art. 110(1)(b): regulation of the borrowing of money or the giving of any guarantee by the Government of India.

Memory hook: **Contingency Fund → custody only. Consolidated Fund → custody + appropriation + charged expenditure.**

questions.stem:
With reference to the election of the President of India, consider the following statements :
1. The value of the vote of each MLA varies from State to State.
2. The value of the vote of MPs of the Lok Sabha is more than the value of the vote of MPs of the Rajya Sabha.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct ?
questions.explanation_md:
Presidential election, **Art. 55** — single transferable vote, proportional representation, uniform scale of representation.

- **Statement 1 — correct.** Value of an MLA's vote = (population of the State ÷ total elected MLAs) ÷ 1000, population taken from the **1971 Census** (frozen till the first census after 2026). So it varies hugely: UP ≈ 208, Sikkim ≈ 7, Arunachal ≈ 8. Different States, different values.
- **Statement 2 — incorrect.** Value of an MP's vote = total value of all MLAs' votes ÷ total number of **elected** MPs (both Houses together). It is a single figure — **currently 700 (708 before the J&K Assembly lapsed)** — and it is **identical for a Lok Sabha MP and a Rajya Sabha MP**. Note: nominated members and MLCs do not vote at all.

**The MP value is one common number for both Houses — it never differs between Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha.** So 1 only.

questions.stem: In the Indian context, what is the implication of ratifying the 'Additional Protocol' with the 'International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA)' ?
options: The civilian nuclear reactors come under IAEA safeguards.
The military nuclear installations come under the inspection of IAEA.
The country will have the privilege to buy uranium from the Nuclear Suppliers Group (NSG).
The country automatically becomes a member of the NSG.
questions.explanation_md:
India signed the **India-specific Additional Protocol with the IAEA in May 2009 and ratified it in June 2014**, as part of the obligations flowing from the 2008 Indo-US civil nuclear deal and the separation plan.

- **(a) Correct.** India follows a **separation plan**: the 14 reactors it designated as civilian are placed under IAEA safeguards; the Additional Protocol extends the IAEA's reporting/access rights over that **civilian** side, chiefly reporting on export of specified nuclear equipment and material.
- **(b) Wrong.** India is a non-NPT nuclear weapon State. Its **military/strategic facilities are permanently outside IAEA inspection** — that was the whole point of the separation plan.
- **(c) Wrong.** Uranium purchase rights came from the **NSG waiver of September 2008**, not from the Additional Protocol. The Protocol is an IAEA instrument, not an NSG one.
- **(d) Wrong.** NSG membership requires consensus of all members; India is still **not a member** (China has blocked it, citing NPT non-signature). Nothing about the Protocol is automatic.

**Additional Protocol = wider IAEA access over the declared civilian side only.**
questions.tagging_note: Straddles international treaty regimes and nuclear science. Tagged CAI-07 primary to match the 2017 Q28 (Nuclear Security Summits) precedent, with SNT-08 for the civil-nuclear/NSG content.

questions.stem:
Consider the following countries :
1. Australia
2. Canada
3. China
4. India
5. Japan
6. USA
Which of the above are among the 'free-trade partners' of ASEAN ?
questions.explanation_md:
ASEAN's **"ASEAN+1" FTA partners** (as of 2018) were six: **China, Japan, South Korea, India, Australia and New Zealand** — exactly the six non-ASEAN countries that were negotiating **RCEP** with ASEAN. Later Hong Kong (AHKFTA, 2019) was added.

Checking the list:
- 1. Australia — **yes** (AANZFTA, 2010, with New Zealand)
- 2. Canada — **no** (only exploring an FTA; not a partner in 2018)
- 3. China — **yes** (ACFTA, 2010)
- 4. India — **yes** (AIFTA goods 2010, services/investment 2015)
- 5. Japan — **yes** (AJCEP, 2008)
- 6. USA — **no** (only a Trade and Investment Framework Arrangement; the US left TPP in 2017)

So **1, 3, 4 and 5**. Shortcut: **the ASEAN FTA partners are precisely the RCEP "+6" — Canada and the USA are not among them.**
questions.tagging_note: Format is a six-item numbered list of countries rather than statements; mapped to stmt_1_2_3 per the numbered-list convention used elsewhere in the bank (the vocabulary has no separate 'numbered list' slug).

questions.stem:
With reference to the 'Global Alliance for Climate-Smart Agriculture (GACSA)', which of the following statements is/are correct ?
1. GACSA is an outcome of the Climate Summit held in Paris in 2015.
2. Membership of GACSA does not create any binding obligations.
3. India was instrumental in the creation of GACSA.
Select the correct answer using the code given below :
questions.explanation_md:
**GACSA** is a voluntary, multi-stakeholder platform (governments, farmers' organisations, NGOs, research bodies, private sector) hosted at **FAO, Rome**.

- **Statement 1 — wrong.** GACSA was launched at the **UN Climate Summit in New York in September 2014**, not the Paris Summit (COP21) of 2015. (Paris 2015 gave the **"4 per 1000" soil initiative**, a different thing — a common trap pairing.)
- **Statement 2 — correct.** Membership is **voluntary and creates no binding obligations**; members simply endorse the framework document and act on their own commitments. This is the defining feature of the Alliance.
- **Statement 3 — wrong.** **India deliberately stayed out of GACSA.** India (with other developing countries and many civil-society groups) was sceptical of "climate-smart agriculture" as a label — fearing it could open the door to mitigation obligations on agriculture and to corporate capture — so India was certainly not instrumental in creating it.

**Voluntary, non-binding, born at New York 2014, and India is not a founder — so 2 only.**
questions.tagging_note: Straddles ENV and GEO. GACSA is an international climate alliance (origin at a UN Climate Summit, voluntary non-binding membership), so ENV-13 climate governance is the primary fit; GEO-17 kept because the subject matter is climate-smart agriculture. Note the 2021 Q59 precedent went the other way (GEO-17 primary) but that question was about India's own agricultural practices, not the alliance.

questions.stem:
Which of the following is/are the aim/aims of "Digital India" Plan of the Government of India ?
1. Formation of India's own Internet companies like China did.
2. Establish a policy framework to encourage overseas multinational corporations that collect Big Data to build their large data centres within our national geographical boundaries.
3. Connect many of our villages to the Internet and bring Wi-Fi to many of our schools, public places and major tourist centres.
Select the correct answer using the code given below :
questions.explanation_md:
**Digital India (launched 1 July 2015)** rests on three vision areas — digital infrastructure as a utility to every citizen, governance and services on demand, digital empowerment of citizens — delivered through **nine pillars**.

- **Statement 1 — wrong.** Nothing in Digital India aims to create **state-backed Indian internet companies on the Chinese model**. China's ecosystem (Baidu, Alibaba, Tencent) grew behind the Great Firewall, which blocks foreign players. Digital India promotes IT/electronics manufacturing and startups broadly, but building India's own walled-garden internet firms is not one of its stated aims.
- **Statement 2 — wrong.** Compelling foreign multinationals to build **data centres inside India (data localisation)** is not a Digital India aim. That debate belongs to the **RBI's 2018 payments-data circular, the Srikrishna Committee and the data protection Bill** — separate from the Digital India programme.
- **Statement 3 — correct.** This is squarely a Digital India pillar: **BharatNet / National Optical Fibre Network to connect 2.5 lakh gram panchayats with broadband**, plus public Wi-Fi hotspots for schools, public places, railway stations and tourist centres. "Broadband Highways" and "Universal Access to Mobile Connectivity" are pillars 1 and 2.

**Only the connectivity statement (3) is an actual stated aim.**
questions.tagging_note: Straddles e-governance and the schemes tracker; POL-27 primary follows the 2016 Q84 (DigiLocker) precedent. Statement 2 (data localisation / data centres) also touches SNT-10, left off to keep the tag honest.

questions.stem:
Consider the following pairs :

| *Towns sometimes mentioned in news* | *Country* |
| --- | --- |
| 1. Aleppo | Syria |
| 2. Kirkuk | Yemen |
| 3. Mosul | Palestine |
| 4. Mazar-i-sharif | Afghanistan |

Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched ?
questions.explanation_md:
Straight place-location recall from the news of 2016-17:

1. **Aleppo — Syria. Correct.** Syria's largest pre-war city; the battle for Aleppo ended in December 2016 with government forces retaking it.
2. **Kirkuk — Yemen. Wrong; it is in IRAQ.** An oil-rich, ethnically mixed (Kurd/Arab/Turkmen) city; the Kurds took it in 2014, Iraqi federal forces retook it in October 2017 after the Kurdish independence referendum.
3. **Mosul — Palestine. Wrong; it is in IRAQ.** ISIS's Iraqi capital, where Baghdadi declared the caliphate in 2014; liberated by Iraqi forces in July 2017.
4. **Mazar-i-Sharif — Afghanistan. Correct.** Capital of Balkh province in the north, site of the Blue Mosque and of the 2017 attack on an Afghan army base.

**Both Kirkuk and Mosul are Iraqi cities, so only pairs 1 and 4 hold.**

questions.stem: In the Federation established by The Government of India Act of 1935, residuary powers were given to the
questions.explanation_md:
The **Government of India Act, 1935** divided powers into three lists — **Federal (59 items), Provincial (54) and Concurrent (36)** — and then broke from the usual federal pattern on the leftover.

**Residuary powers were vested in the Governor-General**, who could authorise either the Federal or a Provincial legislature to enact a law on a subject not in any list. They went to neither legislature.

Contrast for revision:
- **Canada** — residuary power with the Centre; **USA/Australia** — with the States.
- **India, 1950 (Art. 248 + Entry 97, Union List)** — residuary power with **Parliament**.
- **GoI Act 1935** — with the **Governor-General**, in keeping with the Act's general character of leaving discretion and "safeguards" in British hands (the federation itself never came into being; only provincial autonomy did, in 1937).
questions.tagging_note: Straddles POL and HIS. GoI Act 1935 sits in both the Laxmikanth historical-background chapter and Spectrum Ch.18-19; POL-01 primary matches the 2024 Q62 precedent for a 1935-Act provisions question.

questions.stem:
Consider the following statements :
1. The Speaker of the Legislative Assembly shall vacate his/her office if he/she ceases to be a member of the Assembly.
2. Whenever the Legislative Assembly is dissolved, the Speaker shall vacate his/her office immediately.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct ?
questions.explanation_md:
**Article 179** lists the three ways a State Assembly Speaker vacates office.

- **Statement 1 — correct.** Art. 179(a): the Speaker "shall vacate his office if he ceases to be a member of the Assembly." Membership in the House is the foundation of the office. (The other two routes: resignation in writing to the Deputy Speaker, or removal by a resolution of the Assembly passed by a majority of all the then members after 14 days' notice.)
- **Statement 2 — incorrect.** The proviso to Art. 179(a) is the deciding text: **when the Assembly is dissolved, the Speaker does NOT vacate office immediately — he continues until immediately before the first meeting of the newly constituted Assembly.** The office of Speaker is never allowed to fall vacant; continuity is needed to administer the House until the new Speaker is chosen.

Same rule for the Lok Sabha Speaker under **Art. 94**. So **1 only**.
questions.tagging_note: Speaker of a State Legislative Assembly, so POL-21 (state legislature) rather than POL-18; POL-18 retained because the vacation-of-office rule is learned as the parallel of the Lok Sabha Speaker provision (cf. 2025 Q87, tagged POL-18).

questions.stem: Which one of the following reflects the most appropriate relationship between law and liberty ?
options: If there are more laws, there is less liberty.
If there are no laws, there is no liberty.
If there is liberty, laws have to be made by the people.
If laws are changed too often, liberty is in danger.
questions.explanation_md:
A political-theory reasoning question — pick the statement that captures the settled liberal view rather than a popular slogan.

- **(a)** "More laws = less liberty" is the **anarchist/extreme-libertarian** view, and it is false as a general proposition. Laws against assault, fraud and monopoly *create* liberty for everyone else.
- **(b) Correct.** This is the classic position — **Locke: "where there is no law, there is no freedom"; Rousseau, T.H. Green and Laski all argue liberty is a product of a legal order, not its opposite.** Without law there is only the state of nature, where the strong dominate the weak; my freedom exists only because law restrains others from interfering with it. Law is the **condition** of liberty, not merely its limit.
- **(c)** Popular law-making concerns *democratic legitimacy*, a different question from the law-liberty relationship; laws made by the people can still be illiberal (tyranny of the majority).
- **(d)** Frequent change causes uncertainty — a valid but minor, secondary observation, not the "most appropriate relationship".

**Law is the condition of liberty, not its enemy — no law, no liberty.**
questions.tagging_note: VOCABULARY GAP: no topic in topics.json covers abstract political theory (concepts of liberty, law, rights, the liberal-democratic state). This is a conceptual question with no factual anchor in any chapter. POL-03 primary follows the only precedent for this question type (2021 Q90, 'best safeguard of liberty', tagged POL-03 + POL-13); POL-08 added as the nearest substantive home (Right to Freedom, reasonable restrictions). If more such questions appear, the tree may need a POL political-theory node.

questions.stem:
Consider the following statements :
1. No criminal proceedings shall be instituted against the Governor of a State in any court during his term of office.
2. The emoluments and allowances of the Governor of a State shall not be diminished during his term of office.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct ?
questions.explanation_md:
**Art. 361(2): "No criminal proceedings whatsoever shall be instituted or continued against the President, or the Governor of a State, in any court during his term of office."** — Statement 1 correct, and this immunity is absolute for criminal matters (civil suits are allowed after 2 months' notice under 361(4)).

Statement 2 correct: **Art. 158(4)** — the emoluments and allowances of the Governor shall not be diminished during his term of office. Same protection the President gets under Art. 59(4).

Both correct → **(c)**.

Memory hook: for the Governor, *criminal immunity total, salary protected*.

questions.stem: The well-known painting "Bani Thani" belongs to the
questions.explanation_md:
**"Bani Thani" is the signature painting of the Kishangarh school (Rajasthan)** — painted by **Nihal Chand** under the patronage of Raja Sawant Singh (the poet "Nagari Das"), c. mid-18th century.

Identifying features: exaggeratedly elongated face, arched eyebrows, sharply pointed nose and chin, long fish-shaped eyes. Often called the "Indian Mona Lisa"; the model was said to be a singer-poetess in the Kishangarh court, and the pair is depicted as Radha–Krishna.

Distractors: Bundi (lush vegetation, night scenes), Jaipur (Mughal-influenced portraiture), Kangra (Pahari, Gita Govinda themes).

questions.stem: What is "Terminal High Altitude Area Defense (THAAD)", sometimes seen in the news ?
options: A defence collaboration between Japan and South Korea
questions.explanation_md:
**THAAD is a US Army anti-ballistic missile system built by Lockheed Martin** — it intercepts short-, medium- and intermediate-range ballistic missiles in their terminal (final) phase.

Key points: **hit-to-kill, no explosive warhead**; uses an AN/TPY-2 X-band radar. It was in the news over its deployment in **South Korea (Seongju, 2017)**, which China objected to strongly, and later in the UAE/Israel context.

Not Israeli (that's Iron Dome / David's Sling / Arrow), not Indian (that's DRDO's BMD — PAD/AAD, Prithvi Defence Vehicle).
questions.tagging_note: News-driven item about a foreign (US) missile-defence system deployed in South Korea. SNT-07 covers 'missiles, DRDO, stealth' from an Indian-defence angle; the vocabulary has no topic for foreign/global defence systems in the news, so this is the nearest fit rather than an exact one.

questions.stem:
With reference to cultural history of India, consider the following statements :
1. Most of the Tyagaraja Kritis are devotional songs in praise of Lord Krishna.
2. Tyagaraja created several new ragas.
3. Annamacharya and Tyagaraja are contemporaries.
4. Annamacharya kirtanas are devotional songs in praise of Lord Venkateshwara.
Which of the statements given above are correct ?
questions.explanation_md:
1. **Wrong — Tyagaraja's kritis are overwhelmingly in praise of Lord Rama**, not Krishna. This single fact eliminates options (a) and (c).
2. **Correct** — Tyagaraja is credited with composing in and popularising several new/rare ragas (e.g. Kharaharapriya, Harikambhoji among those he brought into currency).
3. **Wrong** — Annamacharya (c. 1408–1503) predates Tyagaraja (1767–1847) by roughly three centuries; not contemporaries. Tyagaraja's contemporaries are Muthuswami Dikshitar and Syama Sastri (the Carnatic Trinity).
4. **Correct** — Annamacharya's sankirtanas are addressed to **Lord Venkateshwara of Tirupati**; he is called "Pada-kavita Pitamaha".

So 2 and 4 only → **(b)**.
questions.tagging_note: Purely Carnatic-music composers (Tyagaraja, Annamacharya) — sits squarely in ART-08. Their devotional-song context brushes the Bhakti movement (ANM-13) but the question tests music history, not Bhakti doctrine.

questions.stem:
Which of the following are regarded as the main features of the "Rule of Law" ?
1. Limitation of powers
2. Equality before law
3. People's responsibility to the Government
4. Liberty and civil rights
Select the correct answer using the code given below :
questions.explanation_md:
Dicey's Rule of Law and its modern expansion cover:
1. **Limitation of powers — correct.** No arbitrary power; government acts only under law (supremacy of law).
2. **Equality before law — correct.** Dicey's second pillar, mirrored in Art. 14.
3. **Wrong — the direction is inverted. Rule of law makes the Government responsible to the people, not the people responsible to the Government.** That single reversal kills (a) and (d).
4. **Liberty and civil rights — correct.** Dicey's third pillar: rights secured through ordinary law and enforced by ordinary courts.

1, 2 and 4 only → **(c)**.
questions.tagging_note: Dicey's Rule of Law is taught in Laxmikanth Ch.7 under Article 14 (equality before law), hence POL-07 primary; it also reads as a salient-feature/constitutional-principle question (POL-03). No dedicated 'rule of law / constitutional principles' topic exists in the vocabulary.

questions.stem: Which one of the following statements correctly describes the meaning of legal tender money ?
options: The money which is tendered in courts of law to defray the fee of legal cases
The money which a creditor is under compulsion to accept in settlement of his claims
The bank money in the form of cheques, drafts, bills of exchange, etc.
The metallic money in circulation in a country
questions.explanation_md:
**Legal tender is money that a creditor is legally bound to accept in discharge of a debt — refusal cannot be used to claim non-payment.** So (b).

In India: **currency notes issued by the RBI are legal tender for unlimited amounts; coins are limited legal tender** (coins up to ₹1 are legal tender up to ₹1,000; the one-rupee note is issued by the Government of India).

Why the others fail: (c) cheques, drafts and bills are **credit/optional money — nobody is compelled to accept them**; (d) metallic money is only one part of legal tender; (a) is a play on the word "tender".

questions.stem: If a commodity is provided free to the public by the Government, then
options: the opportunity cost is transferred from the consumers of the product to the tax-paying public.
the opportunity cost is transferred from the consumers of the product to the Government.
questions.explanation_md:
**Opportunity cost never disappears — it only shifts to whoever actually bears it. A "free" good still uses real resources, and those resources are paid for out of taxes, so the cost moves from the consumer to the tax-paying public.** Hence (c).

(a) is wrong because scarcity is not abolished by a zero price — the land, labour and capital used still had alternative uses. (b) is a value judgement, not an economic consequence. (d) is the trap: the Government is only the conduit; it has no income of its own — **the burden ultimately rests on taxpayers**, not on "the Government".
questions.tagging_note: Tests opportunity cost and who bears the cost of a publicly provided free good — basic microeconomics/public finance. ECO-01 is scoped to national-income aggregates (GDP/GNP/deflator/sectors) and does not actually cover opportunity cost; ECO-10 covers budgets but not this concept either. This is a genuine gap in the syllabus tree: no topic covers introductory micro concepts (scarcity, opportunity cost, public vs private goods).

questions.stem: Increase in absolute and per capita real GNP **do not** connote a higher level of economic development, if
options: industrial output fails to keep pace with agricultural output.
agricultural output fails to keep pace with industrial output.
questions.explanation_md:
**Economic *growth* is a rise in real GNP; economic *development* additionally requires distribution — falling poverty, rising employment, better living standards.** So growth in absolute and per capita real GNP fails to signal development when **poverty and unemployment increase** → (c).

This is the classic "jobless growth" / growth-without-development point: if the extra output is captured by a narrow group, average GNP per head rises while the median person is no better off.

(a), (b) and (d) describe sectoral imbalance or a trade deficit — undesirable, but they do not by themselves contradict a rise in welfare the way rising poverty does.
questions.tagging_note: Growth-versus-development distinction: real GNP rising while poverty and unemployment worsen. ECO-17 carries poverty/unemployment; ECO-01 carries the GNP aggregate.

questions.stem:
Consider the following statements :
Human capital formation as a concept is better explained in terms of a process which enables
1. individuals of a country to accumulate more capital.
2. increasing the knowledge, skill levels and capacities of the people of the country.
3. accumulation of tangible wealth.
4. accumulation of intangible wealth.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct ?
questions.explanation_md:
Human capital formation = investing in **people** — education, training, health, migration, information.

1. **Wrong** — accumulating more *capital* by individuals is physical/financial capital formation, not human capital.
2. **Correct** — it is precisely the process of raising the knowledge, skills and capacities of the population.
3. **Wrong** — tangible wealth (plant, machinery, buildings) is physical capital.
4. **Correct — human capital is intangible: it is embodied in the person and cannot be sold or separated from them.** That contrast between statements 3 and 4 is the whole question.

2 and 4 → **(c)**.
questions.tagging_note: Human capital formation (knowledge, skills, intangible wealth) maps to ECO-18's human-development/education-health scope, though that topic is titled around HDI/MPI indicators rather than human-capital theory.

questions.stem: Despite being a high saving economy, capital formation may **not** result in significant increase in output due to
questions.explanation_md:
**The capital-output ratio (COR) is the units of capital needed to produce one unit of output. A high COR means each rupee of investment yields little extra output — so even heavy saving and investment translate into a small rise in production.** Hence (d).

Harrod-Domar logic: growth rate g = s / v, where s = savings rate and v = capital-output ratio. **A high v directly depresses g however large s is** — that formula is the answer.

Typically COR is high where investment goes into long-gestation, capital-intensive projects (heavy industry, infrastructure) or where capital sits idle. Illiteracy and weak administration hurt efficiency indirectly, but the question asks about capital formation not translating into output, which is definitionally the COR.
questions.tagging_note: Capital-output ratio, savings rate and capital formation are growth-theory concepts (Harrod-Domar), which surface in Five Year Plan models — hence ECO-19 as secondary. No topic in the vocabulary squarely covers economic growth theory / capital formation; ECO-01 is used as the nearest macro-basics bucket. Same gap as Q47.

questions.stem:
After the Santhal Uprising subsided, what was/were the measure/measures taken by the colonial government ?
1. The territories called 'Santhal Paraganas' were created.
2. It became illegal for a Santhal to transfer land to a non-Santhal.
Select the correct answer using the code given below :
questions.explanation_md:
**Santhal Hool (1855–56)**, led by Sidhu and Kanhu Murmu against zamindars, mahajans (dikus) and the Company's police.

**Statement 1 — correct.** After suppression, the government carved out a separate administrative unit, the **Santhal Parganas** (1855, out of Bhagalpur and Birbhum districts), as a **Non-Regulation** area with a special administration under the SPT framework — deliberately insulated from ordinary Bengal regulations.

**Statement 2 — correct.** The whole grievance was tribal land passing to outsider moneylenders. The settlement rules (later codified in the **Santhal Parganas Tenancy Act, 1876/1949**) made **transfer of Santhal land to a non-Santhal illegal**, the same protective logic later used in the Chotanagpur Tenancy Act.

**Both statements are correct → (c).** Memory hook: rebellion → a new territory *plus* a land-alienation bar; the colonial state's standard tribal-pacification package (compare Chotanagpur after Birsa Munda).
questions.transcription_note: 'Santhal Paraganas' is printed exactly so in the booklet (not the conventional 'Parganas'); transcribed as printed.

questions.stem: Economically, one of the results of the British rule in India in the 19th century was the
options: increase in the export of Indian handicrafts
growth in the number of Indian owned factories
rapid increase in the urban population
questions.explanation_md:
**(c) Commercialization of Indian agriculture.**

In the 19th century Indian peasants were pushed into **cash crops for export** — indigo, opium, cotton (boom during the American Civil War, 1861–65), jute, tea, oilseeds — grown for the market rather than for subsistence. Cash revenue demands, the railways, and Britain's need for raw materials drove it. Result: dependence on price swings and reduced food security (a factor in the late-19th-century famines).

Why the others fail:
- **(a)** Indian handicrafts **declined** — de-industrialization; India became an exporter of raw materials and an importer of British machine-made goods.
- **(b)** Indian-owned factories were negligible in the 19th century; modern industry (Tata's mills apart) came mainly after 1900, and even then was small.
- **(d)** Urban population **did not** rise rapidly — old handicraft towns like Dhaka and Murshidabad decayed and people moved *back to land*; India actually saw **ruralization**.
questions.transcription_note: "19th" is printed with a superscript 'th' in the original.

questions.stem: If the President of India exercises his power as provided under Article 356 of the Constitution in respect of a particular State, then
options: the Assembly of the State is automatically dissolved.
the powers of the Legislature of that State shall be exercisable by or under the authority of the Parliament.
Article 19 is suspended in that State.
the President can make laws relating to that State.
questions.explanation_md:
**(b)** Article 356 says that on President's Rule the President may **declare that the powers of the Legislature of the State shall be exercisable by or under the authority of Parliament** — Art. 356(1)(b). That is the exact constitutional text.

Why the others are wrong:
- **(a)** The Assembly is **suspended or dissolved** — dissolution is a choice, not automatic. In *S.R. Bommai* (1994) the SC held the Assembly may only be **suspended** until Parliament approves, and cannot be dissolved before that.
- **(c)** Art. 19 is suspended only during a **National Emergency on ground of war/external aggression** (Art. 358) — never under Art. 356. **Fundamental Rights are not suspended in President's Rule.**
- **(d)** The **President cannot make laws**; Parliament legislates for the State (and may delegate to the President when it is not in session, via ordinance under Art. 357 — but the primary law-making power vests in Parliament, not the President).

questions.stem:
Consider the following pairs :

| *Craft* | *Heritage of* |
| --- | --- |
| 1. Puthukkuli shawls | Tamil Nadu |
| 2. Sujni embroidery | Maharashtra |
| 3. Uppada Jamdani saris | Karnataka |

Which of the pairs given above is/are correct ?
questions.explanation_md:
**Only pair 1 is correct → (a).**

1. **Puthukkuli shawls — Tamil Nadu. Correct.** The coarse white cotton shawl embroidered in red-and-black geometric motifs by the **Toda tribe of the Nilgiris, Tamil Nadu**; carries a **GI tag as "Toda embroidery"**.
2. **Sujni embroidery — Maharashtra. Wrong.** Sujni (Sujani) is a quilted running-stitch embroidery of **Bihar** — Bhusra village, **Muzaffarpur district**, GI-tagged as Sujini embroidery work of Bihar, known for narrative panels on social themes.
3. **Uppada Jamdani saris — Karnataka. Wrong.** Uppada is a coastal village in **East Godavari district, Andhra Pradesh**; the Uppada Jamdani sari holds an **Andhra Pradesh GI tag**.

Hook: the two wrong pairs are both **eastern crafts wrongly shifted west/south** — Sujni is Bihar, Uppada is Andhra.
questions.tagging_note: Vocabulary gap: no ART topic covers handicrafts/textiles/weaving traditions. ART-10 is the nearest fit only because it carries GI tags (Puthukkuli shawls and Uppada Jamdani are GI-tagged). A dedicated crafts/textiles-and-GI topic would be a genuine addition to the tree.
